questions.q: State the formula for the magnitude of the electric field due to an infinitely long straight uniformly charged wire at a perpendicular distance r. Include the SI units of each quantity.
questions.a: E = λ/(2πε₀r), where E is in N/C (or V/m), λ is linear charge density in C/m, ε₀ is permittivity of free space in C²/N·m², and r is perpendicular distance in m. A wrong answer (e.g., E = λ/(4πε₀r²)) reveals confusion with the point charge formula or missing the factor of 2π from the cylindrical surface area.

questions.q: Why is the electric flux through the two flat ends of the cylindrical Gaussian surface zero when calculating the field of an infinite wire? Explain using the relative orientation of the electric field and the area vector.
questions.a: The electric field is radial (perpendicular to the wire), while the area vectors of the flat ends are parallel to the wire axis. Thus E and dS are perpendicular (θ = 90°), so E·dS = 0. A student who says "flux is zero because the ends are far away" misunderstands that flux depends on orientation, not distance.

questions.q: An infinitely long straight wire carries a uniform linear charge density of 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ C/m. Calculate the electric field at a point 5.0 cm from the wire. (Use ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/N·m²)
questions.a:
Given: λ = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ C/m, r = 0.050 m, ε₀ = 8.85 × 10⁻¹² C²/N·m².
Formula: E = λ/(2πε₀r)
Substitute: E = (8.0 × 10⁻⁶) / (2π × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.050)
Compute denominator: 2π × 8.85 × 10⁻¹² × 0.050 = 2.78 × 10⁻¹²
E = 8.0 × 10⁻⁶ / 2.78 × 10⁻¹² = 2.88 × 10⁶ N/C ≈ 2.9 × 10⁶ N/C radially outward.
A wrong answer like 2.9 × 10⁴ N/C suggests a unit error (e.g., using r = 5 cm without converting to metres).

questions.q: Compare the distance dependence of the electric field for: (a) a point charge, (b) an infinite line charge, and (c) an infinite plane sheet. Explain physically why the infinite wire field falls as 1/r while the point charge field falls as 1/r².
questions.a:
(a) Point charge: E ∝ 1/r². (b) Infinite line charge: E ∝ 1/r. (c) Infinite plane sheet: E = constant (independent of r).
The 1/r dependence for the wire arises because the Gaussian surface area (2πrl) grows linearly with r, while the enclosed charge grows linearly with length l. For a point charge, the Gaussian sphere area grows as r², giving 1/r². A student who claims all three follow 1/r² fails to account for how the dimensionality of the charge distribution affects the scaling of the Gaussian surface area.

questions.q: A student uses a spherical Gaussian surface to find the field of an infinite wire and writes: Flux = E × 4πr² = λl/ε₀. They conclude E = λl/(4πε₀r²). Identify the two fundamental errors in this approach.
questions.a:
Error 1: The electric field of an infinite wire is not spherically symmetric; it is cylindrically symmetric. A spherical surface does not have E parallel to dS everywhere, so flux ≠ E × 4πr².
Error 2: The enclosed charge depends on the length l of the wire inside the sphere, which is not simply related to the sphere's radius r. The correct Gaussian surface is a cylinder coaxial with the wire. A student making this error has not internalized that the Gaussian surface must match the symmetry of the charge distribution.

questions.q: Design a thought experiment to verify the 1/r dependence of the electric field of an infinite line charge using only a test charge, a force sensor, and a measuring tape. Describe the procedure, the data to collect, and how you would analyse it to confirm E ∝ 1/r.
questions.a: Procedure: Fix the infinite wire vertically. Place a small positive test charge q on an insulating rod attached to a force sensor. Measure the electrostatic force F on q at several perpendicular distances r (e.g., 10 cm, 20 cm, 30 cm) using the tape. Since E = F/q, plot F vs 1/r. If the data falls on a straight line through the origin, F ∝ 1/r, confirming E ∝ 1/r. A poor answer would measure force at different distances but plot F vs r, missing the inverse relationship.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The electric field due to an infinitely long straight wire with uniform linear charge density λ at a ______ distance r is given by E = λ/(2πε₀r), directed radially outward if λ > 0 and radially inward if λ < 0.
Fill in the blank: Imagine standing near a high-voltage power line (a long ______ wire) — you might wonder how the electric field varies as you move away from it.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student must be able to (1) justify the choice of a cylindrical Gaussian surface using symmetry arguments, (2) compute the electric flux through the curved surface and show flux through the ends is zero, (3) apply Gauss's law to derive E = λ/(2πε₀r), and (4) solve numerical problems involving infinite line charges, including.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine ______ near a high-voltage power line (a long straight wire) — you might wonder how the electric field varies as you move away from it.
